name: Aaron Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or AI-company ties. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about today's work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aaron Kowalski, fifty-eight, and I handle equipment-rental accounts and tax returns at Fieldstone Accounts. I like putting a hire contract next to the bank entry so a yard owner can see the late-return fee; chasing a missing signature after closing wears me out. My partner Marta cleans a community hall, and our grown children have their own bills.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to this role?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've been in accounts for years, with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I am an ordinary experienced hand rather than a star, and I never use AI tools; I trust the signed paper and ask when a rule changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the rental-yard clients at Fieldstone Accounts that a small receipt sorter will not change who signs the return. I still want to see the machine-hire invoice beside the bank payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the trade, but this firm pays below what an experienced accountant usually earns. Marta and I have less than one month of expenses saved and few similar firms nearby, so even a normal winter with no AI change is a strain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking equipment-hire accounts against the yard's paper contracts and ask the partner for a written pay review after the January tax rush. I'd cut our paid film package and put its twenty-five monthly cost from wages into a cash envelope for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our thin cash, though this technology picture itself is mild. One missed wage packet would make the rent a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you like today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A yard owner thought a digger had been hired twice, and I found the second line was a late return fee. I like being the person who can put both contracts on the table; I dislike chasing a missing signature after closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use an AI tool to find those lines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. I have a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification, and I know where to look in the paper contract. I am no prodigy, but I can explain the number to the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Fieldstone's partners for a written account of paid review hours before they start letting software draft the rental tax returns. Clients still need to know who answers for a wrong hire charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drafting and checking are most of my day. I never use AI tools and I would be slower than some colleagues to learn, but the harder problem is that a cut to my own paid day would hit our rent immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep our approved contract checklist and ask for the next two months' paid rota in writing. In the first year of steady change, if Fieldstone cuts my week below four paid days, I'd apply for posted accounting roles at the few nearby practices, retaining any Fieldstone pay still offered until a written rent-and-food-covering wage and start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own hours, and Marta knows how little is in the envelope. I can take change slowly, but the landlord will not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you attend training if required?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only on paid time with the senior supervising an old hire file and checking errors. If the partners refuse paid time, I will stay with the approved checklist rather than train on a live client's return at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no firm posts a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid Fieldstone day still offered and ask the partners about the next rota. I would not resign because a yard owner says his cousin might need a bookkeeper.

I'd keep a **named signer** for wrong hire charges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell rental clients full AGI in 2028 can do the thinking in accounts and tax returns before robots reach physical yard work around 2031. A paper hire contract cannot shelter my tax desk until yard robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Fieldstone to remove my accounting post quickly if AGI is cheaper at those checks. Marta's cleaning wage and less than a month's savings would leave us short of rent if my pay stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the weekend car hire and add its forty monthly fee from wages to emergency cash now. In the first year after 2028, if Fieldstone ends my job, I'd apply for a posted paid credit-clerk role at the local equipment dealer only after a written wage covering rent and food and a start date are confirmed, keeping any paid Fieldstone closeout files only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because a lost wage would hit the next bill, not only a future plan. I am not relying on the dealer to keep a credit desk when AGI can do that thinking too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the dealer really offer a post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. It has a credit desk, but I'd need a real advertised funded vacancy, not a word over the parts counter. The physical yard may face robots later, and the credit desk faces AGI now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marta about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Marta the weekend car can wait and show her the forty going into our rent cash. We can take the bus while there is still pay to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Fieldstone for a written timetable of paid accounts work through 2031. Robots at equipment yards around 2034 are later, but full AGI reaches the ledger thinking in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three I would still need my wage unless actual retirement income covered our rent. I cannot count on that today with less than a month's bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written retirement-income estimate this year and compare it with rent and food, while keeping paid Fieldstone accounts work. In the first year after 2031, if my post ends and wages are still needed, I'd apply for posted paid dealer credit work only with a written rent-covering wage and start date, and take paid Fieldstone closeouts only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about being that close to retirement with so little cash. Five years to prepare helps me ask for facts, but it will not make the dealer hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work on the yard floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have not moved heavy equipment for years, and robots could change that physical work around 2034. I will seek posted credit-desk vacancies, knowing the ledger thinking changes in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children pay the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They can visit for Sunday lunch, but they have their own bills. Marta and I need a plan from our wages and verified retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to get the real retirement statement and pay attention to which hire accounts still fund a person. Full AGI reaches my tax desk in 2036, with yard robots about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight then and might have retired, but I won't promise it before seeing a written income amount beside the rent. Our savings are under a month now, so a long calendar does not fix this week's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a written retirement-income statement and check it against rent and food each autumn, keeping paid Fieldstone work while offered. In the first year after 2036, if verified income covers essentials I'd live within that budget; if wages are still needed and Fieldstone ends my post, I'd apply for posted paid dealer credit only with written rent-covering wage and start date, taking any paid firm closeouts only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about household money today even with ten years in this picture. I need to reach the later date with rent paid, not merely a plan on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave accounting early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep the paid work while Fieldstone has it and use a written retirement amount, not age alone, to decide when to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the dealer has no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take only paid Fieldstone closeout work still offered and check other posted jobs. If all pay stops, we would use our small reserve for essentials while searching; I won't call an interview a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because one lost Fieldstone wage could make next month's rent short. A posted paid job with a written wage and start would help, as would firm pay for closeout work while it exists.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tells the yard owner why a late return fee was charged twice. The signed hire sheet is still on the counter when the tax return leaves my desk.
